metadata.title: Temporal Difference Learning and TD-Gammon
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Reinforcement Learning Paradigm
nodes.statement: A learning agent observes an input state, produces an output action, and receives a scalar reward signal $r$ from the environment. The goal is to generate actions leading to maximal reward.
nodes.statement_clean: A learning agent receives state inputs, produces actions, and learns from a scalar reward signal to maximize cumulative reward.

nodes.name: Temporal Credit Assignment Problem
nodes.statement: When the reward is delayed (given at the end of a long sequence of inputs and outputs), the learner must apportion credit and blame to each of the various inputs and outputs leading to the ultimate final reward signal.
nodes.statement_clean: The problem of distributing credit/blame across a sequence of state-action pairs when the reward is delayed.

nodes.name: Temporal Difference (TD) Learning
nodes.statement: A class of methods in which learning is based on the difference between temporally successive predictions: the goal is to make the current prediction for the current input pattern more closely match the next prediction at the next time step.
nodes.statement_clean: Learning rule that updates predictions toward subsequent predictions, propagating temporal-difference error through time.

nodes.name: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
nodes.statement: A feed-forward neural network in which each node outputs a sigmoidal function of a weighted linear sum of its inputs: $y_j = \sigma\left(\sum_i w_{ij} x_i\right)$, with one or more hidden layers between input and output nodes.
nodes.statement_clean: Feed-forward neural network with one or more hidden layers and sigmoidal squashing activations.

nodes.name: TD-Gammon Input/Output Encoding
nodes.statement: Board positions are encoded as input vectors $x[1], x[2], \ldots, x[f]$. The network output $Y[t]$ is a four-component vector estimating expected outcomes (White/Black winning a normal win or a gammon). Triple-value backgammons are not represented.
nodes.statement_clean: Inputs encode board state (raw checker counts plus optional handcrafted features); output is a 4-vector of win/gammon probabilities for each side.

nodes.name: Equity (Expected Outcome)
nodes.statement: The network's score for a position, interpreted as the estimate of expected outcome of the game from that position. This interpretation is exact in cases where TD($\lambda$) has been proven to converge.
nodes.statement_clean: A position's expected long-run game outcome, used as the value the network estimates.

nodes.name: Slotting Play
nodes.statement: An opening backgammon technique that moves a single checker from the 6 point to the 5 point (e.g., on rolls 2-1, 4-1, 5-1), boldly risking a high probability of being hit in exchange for the opportunity to quickly develop a menacing position if missed.
nodes.statement_clean: Opening play that exposes a checker on the 5 point to risk a hit for positional gain.

nodes.name: Computer Rollout
nodes.statement: A statistical method for quantitatively determining the best move: each candidate position is played to completion several thousand times with different random dice sequences, and the play producing the best outcome statistics is selected.
nodes.statement_clean: Monte-Carlo evaluation of candidate plays by repeated simulated playouts.

nodes.name: Context-Sensitive vs Context-Insensitive Concepts
nodes.statement: A context-insensitive concept assigns a constant value to a feature regardless of other features (e.g., owning the 7 point is always worth a fixed amount). A context-sensitive concept lets the value of a feature depend on the configuration of other features (e.g., the 7 point's value depends on where one's other checkers are).
nodes.statement_clean: Distinction between features whose value is constant vs. features whose value depends on the rest of the position.

nodes.name: TD($\lambda$) Weight Update Rule
nodes.statement: $\Delta w_t = \alpha (Y_{t+1} - Y_t) \sum_{k=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-k} \nabla_w Y_k$, where $\alpha$ is the learning rate, $w$ the weight vector, and $\nabla_w Y_k$ the gradient of network output with respect to weights.
nodes.statement_clean: TD(lambda) update: weight change proportional to temporal-difference error times an exponentially decayed sum of past output gradients.
nodes.notes: Math reconstructed from textual description (PDF→text omitted the displayed equation). Matches Sutton's TD(lambda) formulation cited in [13].

nodes.name: Terminal Update for TD($\lambda$)
nodes.statement: At the end of each game, a final reward signal $z$ is given (4-component, encoding game outcome). The weight-change formula is applied with $(z - Y_f)$ used in place of $(Y_{t+1} - Y_t)$ for the terminal step.
nodes.statement_clean: At terminal time f, replace the TD error $Y_{t+1}-Y_t$ with $z - Y_f$ where $z$ is the actual game outcome.

nodes.name: TD-Gammon Self-Play Training
nodes.statement: Train an MLP evaluation function for backgammon by self-play: at each step the network scores all legal moves, the move with maximum expected outcome is chosen, and weights are updated by TD($\lambda$) using temporally successive predictions; at game end, the actual reward $z$ replaces the next-step prediction.
nodes.statement_clean: Self-play training of a backgammon MLP using TD(lambda) updates between successive predictions, with the terminal outcome as ground truth at game end.
input: Initial neural network with random weights $w$
output: Trained weight vector $w$ defining an evaluation function for backgammon positions

nodes.name: Initialize network
nodes.statement: Initialize the MLP weights $w$ randomly. Initial play is therefore a random strategy.

nodes.name: Generate game by self-play (loop over plies)
nodes.statement: Starting from the opening position, repeat: roll dice; for each legal move, encode the resulting board as $x$ and compute network output $Y$; choose the move with maximum expected outcome for the side to move; advance to the resulting position $x[t+1]$. Continue until a terminal position is reached.

nodes.name: Apply TD($\lambda$) update at each time step
nodes.statement: At each time step $t$, update weights via $\Delta w_t = \alpha (Y_{t+1} - Y_t) \sum_{k=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-k} \nabla_w Y_k$.

nodes.name: Apply terminal update
nodes.statement: At game end, observe outcome reward vector $z$. Apply the weight-update formula with $(z - Y_f)$ replacing $(Y_{t+1} - Y_t)$.

nodes.name: Iterate over many games
nodes.statement: Repeat self-play games (training experience on the order of $10^5$ games for the raw-encoding network) until the evaluation function stabilizes.

nodes.name: Backpropagation
nodes.statement: Supervised gradient-descent procedure for training MLPs by propagating output errors backward through the network to compute weight gradients.
nodes.statement_clean: Standard backpropagation algorithm for supervised MLP training.

nodes.name: Theoretical Doubling Formula
nodes.section: Complexity in the Game of Backgammon (cited)
nodes.statement: A doubling-cube decision rule that consumes TD-Gammon's expected-reward estimates and outputs double/take/drop decisions, added to TD-Gammon after training.
nodes.statement_clean: Post-hoc cube-decision algorithm built on top of TD-Gammon's value estimates.

nodes.name: 2-ply Search Augmentation
nodes.statement: TD-Gammon 2.0 augments the trained evaluation function with a heuristic 2-ply lookahead, evaluating positions reached after a candidate move and the opponent's reply over the dice distribution.
nodes.statement_clean: Add a 2-ply expectimax lookahead on top of the learned evaluator at play time.

nodes.name: Universal Approximation Theorem for MLPs
nodes.statement: Given sufficient hidden units, the multilayer perceptron architecture is capable of approximating any nonlinear function to arbitrary accuracy.
nodes.statement_clean: MLPs with enough hidden units can approximate any nonlinear function to arbitrary accuracy.
conclusions: The MLP can approximate any continuous nonlinear function to arbitrary accuracy

nodes.name: Learning a Backgammon Evaluation Function
nodes.section: Complexity in the Game of Backgammon
nodes.statement: Construct an evaluation function for backgammon positions strong enough to support master-level play, given that exact tables and deep search are infeasible (state space $> 10^{20}$ and a per-ply branching ratio of several hundred).
nodes.statement_clean: Build a backgammon position evaluator competitive with human masters despite the game's enormous state space and branching factor.

nodes.name: Reinforcement Learning with Delayed Reward
nodes.statement: Learn an optimal policy when the reward signal is given only at the end of a long sequence of state-action pairs, requiring solution of the temporal credit assignment problem.
nodes.statement_clean: Generic RL problem with delayed reward and the resulting credit-assignment difficulty.

nodes.name: Raw-Encoding 40-Hidden-Unit Network
nodes.statement: An MLP with 40 hidden units, trained on raw board encoding for 200,000 self-play games via TD($\lambda$), reaches a strong intermediate level of play approximately equal to Neurogammon, despite zero initial knowledge.
nodes.statement_clean: Empirical demonstration: 40-hidden-unit raw-input network trained 200K games matches Neurogammon's level.

nodes.name: Opening Roll 2-1/4-1/5-1: Slot vs Split
nodes.statement: TD-Gammon's rollout analysis showed that on opening rolls 2-1, 4-1, and 5-1, splitting the back checkers (24-23) is superior to the long-favored slotting play (6-5). After the program's analysis appeared in 1992, the split play became the near-universal choice among top players.
nodes.statement_clean: TD-Gammon overturned 30 years of expert opening doctrine by showing the split play beats slotting on 2-1/4-1/5-1.

nodes.name: Sylvester 1988 World Cup Position (4-4 roll)
nodes.statement: In the 1988 World Cup final, Joe Sylvester (top human at the time) played 8-4*, 8-4, 11-7, 11-7 on a 4-4 roll. TD-Gammon recommends the surprising 8-4*, 8-4, 21-17, 21-17. A TD-Gammon rollout confirms its choice gives nearly a tenth of a point of additional equity, suggesting the 17 point is a better advanced anchor than experts had realized.
nodes.statement_clean: Concrete position where TD-Gammon found an unconventional play (advanced anchor at 17) preferable to the consensus expert choice.

nodes.name: TD-Gammon vs Robertie (1992, 51-game test)
nodes.statement: Version 1.0 played 51 games against Robertie, Magriel and Davis, with a net loss of 13 points, an average loss rate of about one-quarter point per game, consistent with Robertie's 0.20-0.25 ppg estimate against world-class human play.
nodes.statement_clean: Empirical match results: TD-Gammon 1.0 lost only ~0.25 ppg vs world-class humans across 51 games.

nodes.name: Absolute vs Relative Accuracy
nodes.statement: TD-Gammon's absolute equity errors are often a tenth of a point or more, yet move selection is master-level because errors across similar candidate positions are highly correlated and effectively cancel when ranking moves.
nodes.statement_clean: Large absolute errors do not impair move ranking because errors on similar positions are highly correlated.

nodes.name: Stochastic Environment Aids Exploration
nodes.statement: Random dice rolls produce variability in training positions, force exploration of the state space, prevent narrow self-reinforcing strategy pathologies, and ensure terminal states are reached, properties that may be missing in deterministic games like chess and Go.
nodes.statement_clean: Stochasticity from dice gives free exploration and guarantees reaching terminal states; deterministic-game self-play lacks both.

nodes.name: Linear Concepts Learned First
nodes.statement: Empirically, the network first learns the linear component of the evaluation function (context-insensitive concepts such as `blots are bad', `points are good'), and only later acquires nonlinear, context-sensitive concepts.
nodes.statement_clean: TD training fits the linear part of the value function early; nonlinearities emerge later.

nodes.name: Smoothness of Value Function for Stochastic Games
nodes.statement: For non-deterministic games the true expected-outcome function is real-valued and smooth; small position changes cause small changes in win probability. Deterministic-game value functions are discrete (win/lose/draw) and presumably harder to learn.
nodes.statement_clean: Stochastic games have smoother target value functions than deterministic ones, which helps function approximation.

nodes.name: Feature Discovery in Hidden Units
nodes.statement: Examination of the input-to-hidden weights of the trained 40-hidden-unit raw-encoding network reveals spatially organized patterns of positive and negative weights resembling features a knowledge engineer might design, demonstrating automatic feature discovery.
nodes.statement_clean: Hidden-unit weights of the trained network correspond to interpretable, hand-engineer-like features.
